endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (iv) the AI is used exclusively for functions such as Service Provider’s internal accounting, human resources, facilities management, or similar back ‑ office purposes.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Governance tools and protocols that are applied to other types of AI systems can be applied to GAI systems. These plans and actions include: • Accessibility and reasonable accommodations • AI actor credentials and qualifications • Alignment to organizational values • Auditing and assessment • Change-management controls • Commercial use

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether defining review scope, limiting expedited review to non-patient-care tools, or requiring use-case descriptions and workflow maps changes how often patient-care AI escapes adequate review. Support for R079 rests on two frameworks, one stated as a requirement and one as an option.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions this is a case of no direct evidence. The two endorsements are frameworks, which are expert judgment rather than empirical findings. Their agreement shows that the practice is accepted, and it does not measure whether the practice works.

The CHAI playbook lists internal accounting, human resources, and facilities management as back-office uses, which gives one working boundary between patient-care and non-patient-care tools. NIST AI 600-1 states that existing governance protocols may be applied to generative AI, and it does not set a review scope. Neither source reports outcomes from applying these scoping rules.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare health systems that use explicit review-scope criteria and restrict expedited pathways with systems that do not. Outcomes should include how many patient-care tools received only expedited or no review, how often tools were reclassified after deployment, and whether workflow maps identified risks before go-live. No such comparison appears in the supplied evidence.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have smaller governance staffs and may rely more on expedited pathways, and whether scoping rules protect their patients has not been examined.
